This graphic map provides a simplified, whimsical overview of the Dublin geography of Ulysses. Zoom in to explore different areas and click on the blue buttons to go to descriptions of locations in the novel. Regrettably, the buttons may not work on mobile devices. Smartphone users may instead have to navigate to the associated chapter and click on the number in square brackets at the top of the text.

Ulysses is a peripatetic novel: nearly every chapter involves some walking. Every chapter but one, however, also centers on one fixed place (tower, school, beach, home, church, cemetery, newspaper office, pub/restaurant, library, hotel bar/restaurant, pub, beach, maternity hospital, brothel, cabman's shelter, home, home), and the total distance covered outside those spaces (within the narrative, as opposed to between chapters) is usually fairly small. The big exception is chapter 10, Wandering Rocks, which takes place in many different locations, beginning with a priest's long walk in the northeast corner of the city and ending with a cavalcade that bisects Dublin from west to east. The image contains two links for this chapter: one where the viceregal carriages leave Phoenix Park, the other where Father Conmee begins his walk at Mountjoy Square. There are two links also for Penelope: one in the house on Eccles Street where Molly lives with Bloom, the other on the Hill of Howth where she became engaged to him.

There are no blue dots in the lower left quadrant of the image because Joyce alludes to the southwestern part of town only rarely and does not center the action of any chapter there. That dead space is livened up with a few images of Joycean interest, but their placement is arbitrary. "U.P.: up," for instance, refers to a postcard that Dubliners are talking about on June 16, not to a billboard south of the Guinness brewery. Similar caveats apply to things like the five men carrying sandwichboards (H, E, L, Y, and ’S) in the northwest part of the city (they actually tramp along Westmoreland Street and Grafton Street in the center of town) and the “Elijah is coming” throwaway floating down the Liffey from the west (it is launched from the O’Connell Bridge in the center of town).

Michael Kirkham designed the image for a jigsaw puzzle called The World of James Joyce, marketed by Laurence King Publishing: www.laurenceking.com/products/the-world-of-james-joyce. Having made use of the Joyce Project while creating the image, Michael asked John Hunt if it could be included on the website as an introduction to the Dublin geography of Ulysses, with navigational hyperlinks added. Rather than trying to link to many different places in the chapters, John proposed connecting to the headnotes that introduce chapters, since those notes attempt, among other things, to orient readers to the times and places of each episode. Users can start with a general overview, focus on some particular part of Dublin, read a headnote describing the action in that part of town, and then begin their own journeys through the text.

John Hunt and Michael Kirkham 2026
